s.q: If a $3\times3$ system with parameters must have infinitely many solutions
s.r: "The system $x+5y-z=1$, $4x+3y-3z=7$, $24x+y+\lambda z=\mu$ has infinitely many solutions; find $\lambda,\mu$".
s.s: Set the coefficient determinant $D=0$; this gives the parameter in the coefficients ($\lambda$). || Find the constant-side parameter ($\mu$) from $D_x=0$ (or $D_y$, $D_z$). || Faster: write the third equation as $p\cdot$(first) $+\,q\cdot$(second); find $p,q$ from two columns, then read $\lambda$ and $\mu$. || If integer solutions are asked, write the general solution with one free variable and impose the conditions.
s.h: Trap: $D=0$ alone does not guarantee infinitely many solutions — it may be inconsistent.

s.q: If the system must have no solution (or a unique solution)
s.r: "Set of $\lambda$ for which the system has no solution", "unique solution for all $\lambda$ except…".
s.s: Compute $D$ as a polynomial in the parameter and find its roots. || For each root, test consistency: compute one $D_i$, or combine the equations to see a contradiction like $x+y+z=6$ and $x+y+z=4$. || Roots that give a contradiction → no solution; roots with all $D_i=0$ → infinitely many (for these simple systems). || Unique solution for all other values.
s.e: $2x-y+2z=2$, $x-2y+\lambda z=-4$, $x+\lambda y+z=4$: $D=-2\lambda^2+\lambda+1=0\Rightarrow\lambda=1,-\frac12$. At $\lambda=1$: (first − second) gives $x+y+z=6$, contradicting the third. Both roots give no solution.

s.q: If lines $ax+by+c=0$ have $a,b,c$ in AP (or another linear relation), so they are concurrent
s.r: "For any three consecutive terms $a,b,c$ of an AP, the lines $ax+by+c=0$ are concurrent at $P$".
s.s: Write the relation as $a\cdot1+b\cdot(-2)+c=0$. || Compare with $ax+by+c=0$: the fixed point is $(x,y)=(1,-2)$. || Use that point in the rest of the problem (system of equations, distance…).
s.e: AP: $2b=a+c$ ⇒ every such line passes through $P(1,-2)$.
